alignment.note: Greek expresses the indefinite relative with the subjunctive plus the particle ἄν (ὃς δ᾽ ἂν βλασφημήσῃ); both the Peshitta (ܕܢܓܕܦ, an imperfect prefixed with relative ܕ) and the Vulgate (blasphemaverit, future-perfect) render the conditional-generic force with a single inflected verb, a routine syntactic compression. The doublet index 2 covers both the Greek particle ἄν and the verb that opens the clause.
εἰς / ܥܠ / in — the Greek and Latin use a directional accusative ('against'), while Syriac ܥܠ ('upon, against') is the standard idiomatic complement for verbs of blaspheming.

Greek attributes holiness with an articular adjective in attributive repetition (τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον) and Latin with a postpositive adjective (Spiritum Sanctum); Syriac employs the construct/genitive ܪܘܚܐ ܕܩܘܕܫܐ ('Spirit of holiness'), a Semitic nominal construction equivalent in sense but distinct in form.

Greek ἔχει and Latin habebit both render 'has/will have' with a transitive verb of possession, whereas Syriac uses the existential particle ܠܝܬ negated ('there is not') together with the prepositional ܠܗ ('to him'), a possessive construction typical of Aramaic which lacks a true verb 'to have'.

Greek (εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) and Latin (in æternum) employ a prepositional phrase 'unto the age/forever'; Syriac compresses this to the single adverbial ܠܥܠܡ, the lexically cognate term (e-l-m, cf. Heb. עוֹלָם) bearing the same temporal sense.
ἔνοχός ἐστιν / ܡܚܝܒ ܗܘ / reus erit — all three predicate guilt with copula plus adjective; the Syriac ܡܚܝܒ (root kh-y-b) carries forensic 'liable/condemned' force matching ἔνοχος and reus.

Greek and Latin read 'guilty of an eternal sin' (αἰωνίου ἁμαρτήματος / æterni delicti), whereas the Peshitta reads ܠܕܝܢܐ ܕܠܥܠܡ, 'liable to eternal judgement/condemnation' (root d-y-n). This is a substantive substitution: Syriac shifts from the offence (the sin itself) to its penal consequence (the judgement), a known interpretive rendering reflecting the variant ἁμαρτίας/κρίσεως debated in the textual tradition.
